title: A context-adaptive policy framework for robust and reactive robotic manipulation via uncertainty-aware imitation learning

3.1 Gaussian Process Regression


Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) [Rasmussen2006] is a probabilistic, non-parametric approach to regression, wherein the latent function is assumed to follow a Gaussian process prior.
Given a set of NN training inputs and the corresponding noisy outputs {𝒔n,𝝃n}n=1N\{\bm{s}_{n},\bm{\xi}_{n}\}^{N}_{n=1},
GPR leverages a joint Gaussian prior over the latent function values.
Here, 𝒔n∈ℝℐ\bm{s}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{I}} specifies the input and 𝝃n∈ℝ𝒪\bm{\xi}_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{O}} denotes the corresponding output
and ℐ\mathcal{I} and 𝒪\mathcal{O} are the dimensions of input and output space.
For a multidimensional output GP with independent output variables and shared hyperparameters across the dimensions,
a posterior predictive distribution for a single test input 𝒔∗\bm{s}_{*} can be derived by conditioning the joint prior on the observed data,
providing both, the mean prediction 𝝁∗∈ℝ𝒪\bm{\mu}_{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{O}} and the associated predictive latent-function variance v∗∈[0,1]v_{*}\in[0,1]:




𝝁∗=𝒌∗⊤​(𝑲+σ2​𝑰N)−1​𝚵,\displaystyle\bm{\mu}_{*}=\bm{k}_{*}^{\top}(\bm{K}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{N})^{-1}\bm{\Xi},

(1)



v∗=k∗∗−𝒌∗⊤​(𝑲+σ2​𝑰N)−1​𝒌∗.\displaystyle v_{*}=k_{**}-\bm{k}_{*}^{\top}(\bm{K}+\sigma^{2}\bm{I}_{N})^{-1}\bm{k}_{*}.

(2)


Here, k∗∗=k​(𝒔∗,𝒔∗)k_{**}=k(\bm{s}_{*},\bm{s}_{*}) denotes the kernel matrix computed at test input 𝒔∗\bm{s}_{*},
𝒌∗=[k​(𝒔∗,𝒔1)⋯k​(𝒔∗,𝒔N)]⊤\bm{k}_{*}=\begin{bmatrix}k(\bm{s}_{*},\bm{s}_{1})&\cdots&k(\bm{s}_{*},\bm{s}_{N})\end{bmatrix}^{\top} is a kernel matrix combining test input and training inputs and




𝑲=[k​(𝒔1,𝒔1)⋯k​(𝒔1,𝒔N)⋮⋱⋮k​(𝒔N,𝒔1)⋯k​(𝒔N,𝒔N)]\bm{K}=\begin{bmatrix}k(\bm{s}_{1},\bm{s}_{1})&\cdots&k(\bm{s}_{1},\bm{s}_{N})\\
\vdots&\ddots&\vdots\\
k(\bm{s}_{N},\bm{s}_{1})&\cdots&k(\bm{s}_{N},\bm{s}_{N})\end{bmatrix}

(3)


refers to the kernel matrix evaluating the similarity of the demonstrated trajectory points.
Moreover, 𝑰N\bm{I}_{N} is an N×NN\times N identity matrix and 𝚵\bm{\Xi} is defined as 𝚵=[𝝃1⋯𝝃N]⊤\bm{\Xi}=\begin{bmatrix}\bm{\xi}_{1}&\cdots&\bm{\xi}_{N}\end{bmatrix}^{\top}.


The kernel function k​(𝒔i,𝒔j)k(\bm{s}_{i},\bm{s}_{j}) is chosen according to the characteristics of the data.
In this work, a unit-amplitude radial basis function (RBF) kernel with k∗∗=1k_{**}=1, given by




k​(𝒔i,𝒔j)=exp​(−12​(𝒔i−𝒔j)⊤​𝑳​(𝒔i−𝒔j)),k(\bm{s}_{i},\bm{s}_{j})=\text{exp}\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\bm{s}_{i}-\bm{s}_{j})^{\top}\bm{L}(\bm{s}_{i}-\bm{s}_{j})\right),

(4)


is used as we assume smooth, continuous trajectories.
The length scales 𝑳=diag​(𝒍)−2\bm{L}=\text{diag}(\bm{l})^{-2}, with 𝒍=[l1​⋯​lℐ]∈ℝℐ\bm{l}=\begin{bmatrix}l_{1}\cdots l_{\mathcal{I}}\end{bmatrix}\ \in\ \mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{I}},
and the noise variance σ2\sigma^{2} denote the hyperparameters of GPR.


The predictive variance of GPR (Eq.˜2) provides a closed-form epistemic uncertainty222Epistemic uncertainty arises from limited knowledge of the model and can be reduced with more data, whereas aleatoric uncertainty reflects inherent stochasticity in the data; see [Huellermeier2021] for an
introduction.
quantification, that increases with the distance to the training data, and therefore helps to identify out of distribution states.

and the inner control loop (highlighted in gray) that makes the robot follow the desired velocities.

5.1 Hyperparameter optimization


Given the influence of GPR hyperparameters on the supplementary policies (e.g., through the shared kernel length over all policies),
the optimization of the combined hyperparameters 𝜽={𝒍,σ2,𝑲sp,𝑲gap}\bm{\theta}=\{\bm{l},\sigma^{2},\bm{K}_{\mathrm{sp}},\bm{K}_{\mathrm{gap}}\} is performed jointly
using the CMA-ES algorithm [Hansen2016], which is used due to its derivative-free nature and its ability to efficiently search complex parameter spaces.
To this end, the skill learning and execution procedure, as summarized in Algorithm˜1, is executed ten times for the provided demonstrations,
while the robot behavior (InnerControlLoop) is simulated by computing the next pose at each time step using 𝒙t+1,i=𝒙t,i+Δ​t​𝒙˙t,i\bm{x}_{t+1,i}=\bm{x}_{t,i}+\Delta t\dot{\bm{x}}_{t,i} and ϕt+1,i=ϕt,i+Δ​t​ϕ˙t,i\bm{\phi}_{t+1,i}=\bm{\phi}_{t,i}+\Delta t\dot{\bm{\phi}}_{t,i}.
To optimize performance both on and off the demonstrated trajectories, the starting poses {𝒙0,k,ϕ0,k}k=110\{\bm{x}_{0,k},\bm{\phi}_{0,k}\}^{10}_{k=1} are sampled randomly within the demonstrated input space,
naturally accounting for sensitivity by evaluating performance across diverse starting poses.
In cases where task-dependent parameters are employed, the recorded values {𝒄m,h}m=1Mh\{\bm{c}_{m,h}\}^{M_{h}}_{m=1} from a random demonstration hh are re-injected into the policy.


Each of the ten simulated trials is terminated when the robot stayed in the goal region for ten iterations (goalReached) or Imax=500I_{\mathrm{max}}=500 iterations are reached.
Defining 𝒑=[𝒙⊤​ϕ⊤]⊤∈ℝ𝒫\bm{p}=\left[\bm{x}^{\top}\>\bm{\phi}^{\top}\right]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{P}} as the end-effector pose,
the robot has reached the goal region if each component p∗,rp_{*,r} of the current end-effector pose 𝒑∗\bm{p}_{*} lies within the distance dr=0.01⋅dmax,rd_{r}=0.01\cdot d_{\mathrm{max},r}
to one of the demonstrated goal poses {𝒑Mh,h}h=1H\{\bm{p}_{M_{h},h}\}^{H}_{h=1},
with dmax,r=maxm,h⁡pm,h,r−minm,h⁡pm,h,rd_{\mathrm{max},r}=\max\limits_{m,h}{p_{m,h,r}}-\min\limits_{m,h}{p_{m,h,r}} describing the max-min range across all demonstrations for the specific entry and r∈[0,𝒫]r\in[0,\mathcal{P}].
We classify trials in which the robot successfully remained in the goal region as successful Sk=1S_{k}=1; otherwise, they are classified as unsuccessful Sk=0S_{k}=0.
Further, we measure the number of iterations ik∈[0,Imax]i_{k}\in[0,I_{\mathrm{max}}] and the mean distance between the executed poses and the closest demonstrated poses across all time steps Dk=1ik​∑j=0ikminm,h⁡‖𝒑m,h−𝒑j‖D_{k}=\frac{1}{i_{k}}\sum_{j=0}^{i_{k}}\min\limits_{m,h}{\left\|\bm{p}_{m,h}-\bm{p}_{j}\right\|}.
We define the multi-objective cost function as an equally weighted sum:




min𝜽⁡J=(1−S)+IImax+D∑r=1𝒫dmax,r2,\min_{\bm{\theta}}{J}=(1-S)+\frac{I}{I_{\mathrm{max}}}+\frac{D}{\sqrt{\sum_{r=1}^{\mathcal{P}}d_{\mathrm{max},r}^{2}}},

(13)


where, SS, II and DD are the average success, iterations and distance over ten trials, thus all objectives lie within [0,1][0,1].
We further constrain the search space of the hyperparameters in 𝜽\bm{\theta} to 1% - 100% of their respective max-min ranges.


The hyperparameters for the LASA handwriting dataset experiment (Section˜5.2) are obtained within 500 optimization iterations using a combined objective function and a single set of hyperparameters for all letters.
As the robot state and action spaces remain the same, we optimize the hyperparameters for the real-robot experiments (Sections˜5.3, 5.4 and 5.6) over 500 optimization iterations using the training data of the experiment described in Section˜5.6
and then manually refined the task-parameter-dependent kernel length for the experiments described in Sections˜5.3 and 5.4, as only the domain of 𝒄\bm{c} varies across tasks.
Starting from the CMA-ES-derived initial value (Section˜5.6), l𝒄l_{\bm{c}} was tuned via a unit-step search within the bounds of the demonstrated 𝒄\bm{c} range.
Each candidate value was evaluated over five independent trials initialized at the demonstrated start poses.
The parameter was incremented until entering, and subsequently leaving, the region of 100% success rate,
thereby identifying the contiguous interval of tested values achieving perfect success.
The final value of l𝒄l_{\bm{c}} was chosen as the median of this interval.
This criterion emphasizes operational robustness and is consistent with our sensitivity analysis (Appendix˜C),
which indicates approximately symmetric performance degradation around the unperturbed value, confirming robustness against 𝒄\bm{c} perturbations up to ±2.5​N\pm 2.5\,\text{N}.
We selected this strategy as it provides a fast and practical solution,
while a direct optimization of the hyperparameters, as for 5.6, would also be possible.
